text: Selenium is a chemical element with the symbol Se and atomic number 34. It exhibits various physical forms, including a brick-red powder, a vitreous black solid, and a grey metallic-looking form. It rarely occurs in its elemental state or as pure ore compounds in Earth's crust. The element, named from σελήνη ('moon'), was discovered in 1817 by Jöns Jacob Berzelius, who observed its similarity to tellurium, which was named for the Earth. Berzelius and Johan Gottlieb Gahn, both operating a sulfuric acid production plant near Gripsholm, Sweden, noticed a red precipitate from pyrite samples from the Falun Mine; when burned, it emitted a horseradish-like odor, not typical of arsenic but similar to tellurium. Berzelius initially thought it was a tellurium compound but later reanalyzed it and concluded it was a new element, naming it after the Moon due to its similarity to tellurium. Selenium is found in metal sulfide ores, where it substitutes for sulfur, and is commercially produced as a byproduct during the refining of these ores. Pure selenide or selenate minerals are rare. The primary commercial uses today are in glassmaking and pigments, while selenium's semiconductor properties have historically been used in photocells and electronics, though these applications have largely been replaced by silicon-based devices. Selenium is still used in a few types of DC power surge protectors and one type of fluorescent quantum dot. Trace amounts of selenium are essential for cellular function in many animals, including humans, and are components of antioxidant enzymes such as glutathione peroxidase and thioredoxin reductase, as well as three deiodinase enzymes. Selenium requirements vary among plant species. Selenium has several allotropes that interconvert with temperature changes; when prepared in chemical reactions, it is usually an amorphous brick-red powder. Rapid melting produces black, vitreous selenium, sold commercially as beads, which has an irregular, complex structure with polymeric rings containing up to 1000 atoms per ring, is brittle and lustrous, slightly soluble in CS2, softens at 50 °C, and converts to gray selenium at 180 °C—this temperature is reduced by halogens and amines. The red α, β, and γ forms are produced by varying the evaporation rate of solvent (usually CS2) from black selenium solutions and all have low monoclinic crystal symmetry (space group 14) with nearly identical puckered Se8 rings, where the Se–Se distance averages 233.5 pm and the Se–Se–Se angle is 105.7°; the eight atoms in a ring are not equivalent, and in the γ form, half the rings are in one configuration and its mirror image. The packing is densest in the α form. Other allotropes may contain Se6 or Se7 rings. The most stable and dense form is gray selenium, with a chiral hexagonal crystal lattice (space group 152 or 154), consisting of helical polymeric chains, where the Se–Se distance is 237.3 pm and the Se–Se–Se angle is 103.1°, with a minimum chain-to-chain distance of 343.6 pm. Gray selenium is formed by mild heating, slow cooling of molten selenium, or condensing selenium vapor just below its melting point; it is a semiconductor with appreciable photoconductivity, insoluble in CS2, resistant to oxidation by air and nonoxidizing acids, and forms polyselenides with strong reducing agents. It does not exhibit the viscosity changes sulfur does when heated. Selenium has seven naturally occurring isotopes: five—74Se, 76Se, 77Se, 78Se, and 80Se—are stable, with 80Se being the most abundant (49.6% natural abundance), and 82Se, a long-lived primordial radionuclide with a half-life of 8.76×10¹⁹ years, is also naturally occurring. The non-primordial isotope 79Se occurs in minute quantities in uranium ores from nuclear fission. Numerous unstable synthetic isotopes range from 64Se to 95Se; the most stable are 75Se (half-life 119.78 days) and 72Se (half-life 8.4 days). Isotopes lighter than stable ones undergo beta plus decay to arsenic isotopes, and heavier ones undergo beta minus decay to bromine isotopes, with minor neutron emission in the heaviest isotopes. Selenium commonly exhibits oxidation states of −2, +2, +4, and +6 and is classified as a nonmetal (rarely considered a metalloid) with properties intermediate between sulfur and tellurium and similarities to arsenic. It forms two oxides: selenium dioxide (SeO2), produced by combustion of elemental selenium, which is a polymeric solid forming monomeric SeO2 molecules in the gas phase and dissolves in water to form selenous acid (H2SeO3), which can also be made by oxidizing elemental selenium with nitric acid; selenium trioxide (SeO3) is thermodynamically unstable and decomposes above 185 °C, and is produced in the lab by reacting anhydrous potassium selenate with sulfur trioxide. Selenous acid salts are called selenites, including silver selenite (Ag2SeO3) and sodium selenite (Na2SeO3). Hydrogen sulfide reacts with aqueous selenous acid to produce selenium disulfide, which consists of 8-membered rings with approximate composition SeS2, including variations like Se4S4 and Se2S6; it is used in shampoos as an antidandruff agent, in polymer chemistry, as a glass dye, and as a reducing agent in fireworks. Selenium trioxide can be synthesized by dehydrating selenic acid (H2SeO4), produced by oxidizing selenium dioxide with hydrogen peroxide. Selenium reacts with fluorine to form selenium hexafluoride (SeF6), which is more reactive and a toxic pulmonary irritant than sulfur hexafluoride; selenium tetrafluoride is a laboratory-scale fluorinating agent. The only stable chlorides are selenium tetrachloride (SeCl4) and selenium monochloride (Se2Cl2), structurally analogous to disulfur dichloride; metastable solutions of selenium dichloride can be prepared from sulfuryl chloride and selenium and are important in preparing selenium compounds like Se7; corresponding bromides are known and follow similar stability and structure. Iodides of selenium are poorly known and were long believed not to exist; limited spectroscopic evidence suggests lower iodides may form in bi-elemental solutions with nonpolar solvents like CS2 or CCl4, but they decompose under illumination. Some selenium oxyhalides—seleninyl fluoride (SeOF2) and selenium oxychloride (SeOCl2)—are used as specialty solvents. Selenium forms hydrogen selenide (H2Se), a strongly odiferous, toxic, colorless gas more acidic than H2S, which ionizes to HSe−; the selenide dianion (Se2−) forms compounds such as mercury selenide (HgSe), lead selenide (PbSe), zinc selenide (ZnSe), and copper indium gallium diselenide (Cu(Ga,In)Se2), all of which are semiconductors. With highly electropositive metals like aluminum, these selenides are prone to hydrolysis. Alkali metal selenides react with selenium to form polyselenides (Se2−n) as chains and rings. Tetraselenium tetranitride (Se4N4) is an explosive orange compound analogous to tetrasulfur tetranitride (S4N4), synthesized by reacting selenium tetrachloride with [((CH3)3Si)2N]2Se. Selenium reacts with cyanides to yield selenocyanates. Selenium, especially in the +2 oxidation state, forms organic derivatives such as selenides (R2Se), diselenides (R2Se2), and selenols (RSeH), analogous to organosulfur compounds; examples include selenomethionine, diphenyldiselenide, and benzeneselenol. Selenoxides (RSe(O)R) are intermediates in organic synthesis, such as in the selenoxide elimination reaction; selenoketones and selenaldehydes are rarely observed. In 1873, Willoughby Smith discovered that the electrical conductivity of gray selenium is affected by light, leading to its use in light-sensing cells. Werner Siemens developed the first commercial selenium-based products in the mid-1870s, and the selenium cell was used in Alexander Graham Bell’s photophone in 1879. Selenium transmits an electric current proportional to the light intensity, used in light meters and similar devices. Selenium rectifiers were developed in the early 1930s and replaced copper oxide rectifiers due to higher efficiency, remaining in use until the 1970s when they were replaced by silicon rectifiers. Selenium gained medical attention due to its toxicity in industrial workers and as a veterinary toxin in animals consuming high-selenium plants. In 1954, Jane Pinsent discovered specific biological functions in microorganisms; it was shown to be essential for mammalian life in 1957. In the 1970s, selenium was found in two sets of enzymes, and selenocysteine in proteins was discovered; by the 1980s, it was shown that selenocysteine is encoded by the UGA codon, with the recoding mechanism first identified in bacteria and later in mammals (via the SECIS element). Native selenium is a rare mineral, forming steep rhombohedra or tiny acicular crystals when present. Selenium occurs naturally in selenide, selenate, and selenite forms, but these minerals are rare; the common mineral selenite is not a selenium mineral and is actually a type of gypsum (calcium sulfate hydrate) named for the Moon before selenium was discovered. Selenium is most commonly found as a sulfur substitute in sulfide ores of metals like copper, nickel, or lead. It is isolated from anode mud in copper refining and from lead chamber process muds, though the latter process is no longer used. Most elemental selenium is produced as a byproduct of copper refining or sulfuric acid production. Solvent extraction and electrowinning (SX/EW) in copper production now accounts for a growing share of global copper supply, reducing selenium availability since only a small portion of selenium in the ore is leached with copper. Industrial production typically involves extracting selenium dioxide from copper purification residues, oxidizing it with sodium carbonate to form selenium dioxide, mixing with water and acidifying to form selenous acid, and then bubbling with sulfur dioxide to produce elemental selenium. In 2011, about 2,000 tonnes of selenium were produced worldwide, primarily in Germany (650 t), Japan (630 t), Belgium (200 t), and Russia (140 t), with total reserves estimated at 93,000 tonnes—data excluding the United States and China. The price rose sharply from $4–$5 to $27/lb in 2004, remained stable at about $30/lb from 2004 to 2010, and increased to $65/lb in 2011. Consumption in 2010 was divided as: metallurgy (30%), glass manufacturing (30%), agriculture (10%), chemicals and pigments (10%), and electronics (10%). China is the dominant consumer, using 1,500–2,000 tonnes per year. During manganese electrowinning, selenium dioxide is added to reduce power consumption; China is the largest consumer of selenium dioxide, using an average of 2 kg per tonne of manganese.

Selenium reserves are estimated at 93,000 tonnes, with production from Russia (140 t) and another country (not specified) excluded, and the United States and China being the two major producers not included in these data. The price of selenium saw a sharp increase from $4–$5 to $27/lb in 2004, then remained stable at about US$30 per pound (in 100-pound lots) from 2004 to 2010, rising to $65/lb in 2011. In 2010, consumption was divided as follows: metallurgy – 30%, glass manufacturing – 30%, agriculture – 10%, chemicals and pigments – 10%, and electronics – 10%. China is the dominant consumer, using 1,500–2,000 tonnes per year. During electrowinning of manganese, selenium dioxide reduces the power needed for electrolysis, with China being the largest consumer of selenium dioxide for this purpose; approximately 2 kg of selenium oxide is used per tonne of manganese. About 50% of selenium consumption is for glass production, where selenium compounds provide a red color that counteracts green or yellow tints from iron impurities, using selenite and selenate salts; red color can also be achieved through mixtures of CdSe and CdS. Selenium is used with bismuth in brasses to replace lead, driven by the Safe Drinking Water Act of 1974, resulting in the development of EnviroBrass; like lead and sulfur, selenium improves steel machinability at around 0.15% and similarly enhances copper alloy machinability. In the 2010s, the lithium–selenium (Li–Se) battery was considered for energy storage. Selenium was the photoabsorbing layer in the first solid-state solar cell demonstrated by William Grylls Adams and Richard Evans Day in 1876, and Charles Fritts later built the first thin-film solar cell using selenium; however, silicon solar cells emerged in the 1950s, leading to a decline in selenium research, with the record efficiency of 5.0% set by Tokio Nakada and Akio Kunioka in 1985 remaining unchanged for over 30 years. In 2017, IBM researchers achieved a new efficiency of 6.5% through device redesign, sparking renewed interest in selenium as a wide bandgap photoabsorber for tandem cells; in 2024, the first selenium-based tandem solar cell was demonstrated with a selenium top cell monolithically integrated with a silicon bottom cell, though a significant deficit in open-circuit voltage remains the main efficiency barrier, requiring defect-engineering strategies, particularly for carrier lifetime; recent first-principles defect calculations show selenium has intrinsic point defect tolerance, with interfaces and extended defects being the primary performance limitations; the only investigated defect-engineering strategy involves laser crystallization of selenium thin films. Amorphous selenium (α-Se) thin films are used as photoconductors in flat-panel X-ray detectors, converting X-ray photons directly into electric charge due to favorable technological and physical properties. Selenium rectifiers were first used in 1933 and are mostly replaced by silicon-based devices, except in power DC surge protection where selenium suppressors are preferred due to superior energy capabilities. Demand from the electronics industry is declining, though selenium remains useful in photocopying, photocells, light meters, and solar cells; its use as a photoconductor in copiers declined in the 1980s as organic photoconductors became more common. Zinc selenide was the first material for blue LEDs, though gallium nitride dominates; cadmium selenide is used to make quantum dots. Amorphous selenium sheets convert X-ray images into charge patterns in xeroradiography and solid-state, flat-panel X-ray cameras. Ionized selenium (Se+24) is used in X-ray lasers, and 75Se is used as a gamma source in industrial radiography. Selenium catalyzes some chemical reactions but is not widely used due to toxicity. In X-ray crystallography, selenium atoms replacing sulfur aid in multiple- and single-wavelength anomalous dispersion phasing. Selenium is used in photographic print toning, intensifying and extending tonal range and improving print permanence; small amounts of organoselenium compounds modify rubber vulcanization catalysts. Selenium disulfide is used in anti-dandruff shampoos such as Selsun and Vichy Dereos. Selenium pollution affects aquatic systems due to farming runoff and industrial processes; people who eat more fish are generally healthier, suggesting no major human health concern, though selenium has potential effects. Selenium poisoning occurs when agricultural runoff leaches soluble selenium compounds (e.g., selenates) into water, which concentrates in wetlands during evaporation, or from coal flue ash, mining, metal smelting, crude oil processing, and landfills; high selenium levels cause congenital disorders in oviparous species like wetland birds and fish, with elevated methylmercury levels amplifying toxicity. Selenium bioaccumulates in aquatic habitats, with zooplankton concentrating organoselenium compounds over 200,000 times at 0.5–0.8 μg Se/L, and phytoplankton concentrating inorganic selenium by 3000 times; bioaccumulation continues through the food chain. A water concentration of 2 μg Se/L is considered highly hazardous to sensitive fish and aquatic birds; selenium poisoning can be passed from parents to offspring and persist across generations; reproduction in mallard ducks is impaired at 7 μg Se/L, and many benthic invertebrates tolerate up to 300 μg/L. Fish kills occur due to selenium bioaccumulation, with some species surviving; seasonal factors may influence harm. High selenium tissue concentrations cause gill swelling, reduced oxygen diffusion, hemoglobin binding, liver degeneration, heart swelling, damaged egg follicles, cataracts, and fluid accumulation; malformed fetuses with feeding or breathing issues and fin or spine distortions are common; adult fish may appear healthy but be unable to produce viable offspring. In Belews Lake, North Carolina, 19 fish species were eliminated between 1974 and 1986 due to 150–200 μg Se/L wastewater from a Duke Energy coal-fired power plant; at the Kesterson National Wildlife Refuge in California, thousands of fish and waterbirds were poisoned by selenium in agricultural irrigation drainage. Selenium is an essential micronutrient for animals, occurring as a bystander mineral in plants, sometimes in toxic amounts in forage (some plants accumulate selenium as a defense, while others like locoweed require it); human body selenium content is estimated at 13–20 mg. Selenium is a component of selenocysteine and selenomethionine, and in humans, it functions as a cofactor for antioxidant enzymes such as glutathione peroxidases and certain thioredoxin reductases. The glutathione peroxidase family removes reactive oxygen species like hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides. The thyroid gland and all cells using thyroid hormones use selenium as a cofactor for three of the four known thyroid hormone deiodinases, which activate and deactivate thyroid hormones and metabolites. Increased dietary selenium reduces mercury toxicity, especially at low to moderate mercury doses, through irreversible inhibition of selenoenzymes involved in preventing oxidative damage in brain and endocrine tissues; selenoneine is present in bluefin tuna blood. Certain plants, including Astragalus species, prince's plume, woody asters, and false goldenweed, are indicators of high selenium soil content. Dietary selenium comes from meat, nuts, cereals, and mushrooms, with Brazil nuts being the richest source (soil-dependent). The US RDA for teenagers and adults is 55 μg/day; selenium supplements typically contain 55 or 70 μg per serving in multi-vitamins and 100 or 200 μg in selenium-specific supplements. In June 2015, the FDA established minimum and maximum selenium levels in infant formula. Exceeding the Tolerable Upper Intake Level of 400 μg/day can lead to selenosis; this level is based on a 1986 study of five Chinese patients and a 1992 follow-up that found a safe intake of about 800 μg/day (15 μg/kg body weight), though 400 μg/day was recommended to avoid nutrient imbalance and account for international data. In China, people consuming corn grown in selenium-rich stony coal (up to 9.1% selenium) have suffered toxicity. Symptoms of selenosis include garlic breath, gastrointestinal issues, hair loss, nail sloughing, fatigue, irritability, and neurological damage; extreme cases can lead to liver cirrhosis, pulmonary edema, and death. Elemental selenium and most metallic selenides have low toxicity due to low bioavailability, while selenates and selenites are highly toxic with oxidant properties similar to arsenic trioxide; the chronic toxic dose of selenite is 2400–3000 μg/day. Hydrogen selenide is an extremely toxic, corrosive gas. Organic selenium compounds like dimethyl selenide, selenomethionine, selenocysteine, and methylselenocysteine are highly bioavailable and toxic in large doses. OSHA and NIOSH both set an 8-hour workday permissible exposure limit of 0.2 mg/m³ for selenium; at 1 mg/m³, selenium is immediately dangerous to life and health. Selenium can be measured in blood, plasma, serum, or urine to monitor exposure, confirm poisoning, or assist in forensic investigations; analytical techniques can distinguish organic from inorganic forms; both forms are largely converted to selenosugars before excretion. Cancer patients on daily selenothionine doses may achieve very high plasma and urine selenium levels. Selenium deficiency occurs in patients with severely compromised intestinal function, those on total parenteral nutrition, and those over 90, as well as people relying on food from selenium-deficient soil; New Zealand, with low soil selenium, has not shown adverse health effects. Selenium deficiency defined by low (<60% of normal) selenoenzyme activity in brain and endocrine tissues only occurs when combined with additional stressors such as high mercury exposure or vitamin E deficiency. Selenium interacts with iodide and vitamin E, influencing deficiency diseases in animals, though pure selenium deficiency is rare. The health effects of selenium deficiency remain uncertain, particularly regarding Kashin-Beck disease. Selenium may have a chemo-preventive role in cancer due to its antioxidant properties and immune stimulation; at low levels, it forms anti-oxidant selenoproteins, and at higher doses, it induces cell death. Selenium, in conjunction with iodine, supports thyroid health by acting as a cofactor for thyroid hormone deiodinases, which activate and deactivate thyroid hormones; isolated selenium deficiency is being studied for its potential role in triggering autoimmune reactions in Hashimoto’s disease; combined iodine and selenium deficiency has been shown to have a thyroid-protective effect.

Selenium is involved in the body's production of antioxidant selenoproteins, and at doses above normal levels, it can lead to cell death.[148] It works in conjunction with iodine to support thyroid health, serving as a cofactor for the three thyroid hormone deiodinases, which are responsible for activating and deactivating thyroid hormones and their metabolites. Research suggests that isolated selenium deficiency may contribute to autoimmune reactions in the thyroid gland, particularly in Hashimoto's disease.[149] Additionally, a case study demonstrated that combined iodine and selenium deficiency has a thyroid-protecting effect.[150]
